messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan was a 21-year-old European American man who had been married for just over a year and was currently unemployed, spending most of his days at home and in the small circle of errands he felt able to manage. His difficulties were traced to a traumatic event that had involved someone he loved rather than himself: the violent injury of his older brother during a late-night assault that Ethan had witnessed enough of to leave him with vivid, enduring impressions. He still described the moment as split into pieces he could not put into words. When he tried to tell the story, he would stop and say he could not explain it properly, that it was less like a memory than a series of photographs that kept appearing in his mind. One image in particular stayed fixed: a close, unmistakable view of a body part that had become tied to the event, something he could not now see without feeling sick and alert. Even years later, if he thought about that night, he sometimes caught the same sharp, dirty smell in his mind that had been in the air then, and he would pause as if the room around him had changed.

In the weeks after the assault, Ethan found that certain moments outside his control brought the event back with surprising force. If someone moved suddenly near him, even in a harmless way, he was immediately on guard, his whole body bracing before he had time to think. He described scanning people for signs that they were acting suspiciously, as though any odd glance, hesitation, or approach from the wrong person might mean trouble. Comments about family were especially difficult. If someone asked where his brother was, made a remark about siblings, or spoke casually about “family stuff,” Ethan became tense and withdrawn, because those comments seemed to pull him back toward the night when his family had been fractured by violence. He also noticed that the visual reminder of that specific body part from the event could catch him off guard, making him feel as though he were right back in the moment rather than safely in his present life.

As the months passed, Ethan began organizing his life around keeping those feelings from erupting. He stopped watching TV programmes and films or reading anything that resembled the assault, no matter how indirectly. News stories, dramas, or even articles with similar themes were avoided because he did not trust himself to stay calm if they resembled what had happened. He also tried hard not to be alone in a room or building. When his wife went out, he often stayed close to the door, called family more often, or found reasons to leave the house rather than sit by himself. Being alone made him feel exposed, as if there would be no one there if he suddenly felt himself slipping back into the event. On several occasions, when the feelings became overwhelming and he felt unable to settle, he hurt himself physically to release the pressure. He did not present this as a wish to die so much as an urgent attempt to force his mind and body to discharge what felt unbearable.

Ethan’s sleep had become fractured as well. He described trouble falling asleep and staying asleep, partly because bedtime left too much space for what his mind might do. When he did drift off, he was sometimes startled awake feeling as if the frightening experience were happening again, with his body reacting before he had fully oriented to the room. In those moments he was not simply remembering; he would briefly act as though danger was present now. He had come to believe that his body kept reacting as if he were still in danger even when he was safe, and this unsettled him because it made safety feel unreliable. He was also increasingly convinced that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him before all of this. The loss was not only about the traumatic event itself but about his sense of who he had been able to be. He spoke with frustration and shame about not trusting himself anymore, saying he could not rely on himself the way he once had.

By the time he came for help, Ethan and his wife had begun to notice how much his world had shrunk. His unemployment left him with long stretches at home, which made it harder to distract himself and easier for him to fall into the habits of checking the environment, avoiding media, and steering clear of being alone. He wanted help because he was tired of living as though any sudden movement, suspicious look, or remark about family might turn into the worst night of his life again. What he most feared was losing more of his life to these reactions, and what he most hoped for was a way to feel like himself again without having to stay on guard every waking moment.
